newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Best on Ground-Andrew Bartram's Aussie Rules column.
newsitem.headline: Best on Ground-Andrew Bartram's Aussie Rules column.

text.p: AUSSIE RULES
CHANGING OF THE GUARD

For nearly a century Victorian clubs dominated Australian Rules football and when the AFL was established in 1991 there was a lamentable outcry from traditionalists about the abdication of loyalty to Victoria, the game's birth place.

Six years hence, and with just four games to complete the 1997 home and away season, five out of six interstate clubs are poised in the top eight, pushing the league's traditional Melbourne powerbrokers down the ladder in the process.

The current situation proves unequivocally that Aussie Rules is now truly a national game and Victorians can do no more than mourn the passing of a glorious era and rejoice, or at least accept, that a new one has begun.
Indeed, that era began in 1992 when West Coast defeated Geelong in the grand final to be the first so-called expansion team to climb AFL's Mount Everest.

Who's to say the Eagles won't do it again this year. Since Hawthorn's decline, the Eagles have been regarded as the competition's measuring stick but some un-Eagle like performances this year, particularly a string of successive losses and an inability to win in Melbourne, have pundits questioning their credentials.

Adelaide was always dismissed as an AFL heavyweight because of its inability to win away from Football Park but this year the Crows boast the best road record in the competition and loom as a genuine premiership chance.

Like Sydney, the Crows play three of their last four games at home before a last round encounter with Essendon at Optus Oval. Four straight wins could give the Crows top spot if incumbent Geelong falters in the run home.

Nothing is certain in this game but if, as expected, the Swans win all their remaining home games and topple Carlton at Optus Oval in round 21, they should finish in the top two and secure two home finals at the SCG where they are unbeaten in 19 games.

Pre-season premiership favorites Brisbane will sneak into the finals but it could be a brief campaign for the Lions who have lost Voss and Molloy to knee injuries and face the prospect of a final outside Queensland. Like Guinness the Lions don't travel well.
The fifth interstate club to figure in the fight for the final eight will be the fledgling Port Adelaide which may sneak in ahead of the Western Bulldogs.

The Power have a tough finish ahead of them with games against Adelaide and St Kilda at Football Park and away games against Brisbane and Richmond and to pinch a finals berth will be a wonderful achievement.

Western Bulldogs, on top of the ladder four weeks ago but winless since and now ninth, have a more favorable draw and, provided they can return to the form they showed earlier, should grab eighth spot with a game in hand.
They, along with ladder leader Geelong, reigning premier North Melbourne and St Kilda should make up the remainder of the final eight.
WALLACE'S MEN LOOK DOG-TIRED
Speaking of the Western Bulldogs, most AFL players will be breathing a sigh of relief at their alarming form slump following four consecutive losses.

The Dogs broke with convention by starting their pre-season immediately after the Grand Final. With 10 wins from their first 14 games the plan looked to have paid dividends and most opposition players were bracing themselves for the longest of pre-seasons.
Ever the innovator, Bulldog coach Terry Wallace may be forced back to the drawing board. His players look burned-out, even dog-tired.
On Saturday Richmond continued the Bulldog's nightmare and also became the 10th of 12 teams since 1978 to win the week after sacking its coach.
In round 10, Melbourne became the ninth when it beat Richmond by 25 points only days after sacking Neil Balme.
*Andrew Bartram will be writing a regular AFl column for Reuters. Any feedback to michael.stapleton@reuters.com
